title: Distributed Key-Value Store
summary: Build a durable, partitioned key-value storage engine with tunable consistency.
statement:
Design a distributed, disk-backed key-value storage system that persists data reliably across machine failures and scales horizontally as capacity grows.

Functional requirements:
- Support `put(key, value)`, `get(key)`, and `delete(key)` for keys up to 1 KB and values up to 1 MB.
- Persist writes durably on disk so committed data survives process restarts and single-node hardware failures.
- Allow callers or table configs to trade latency against consistency for reads and writes.
- Add or decommission storage nodes without downtime.

Scale to assume:
- 200 TB of logical data before replication.
- 1 million writes per second and 2 million reads per second across the cluster.
- Single-digit millisecond median latency within a region.
hints: Look at what happens inside a single storage node first: how do you make random writes fast on disk while still keeping reads efficient?
Once keys are partitioned and replicated across `N` nodes, how do write (`W`) and read (`R`) quorum sizes control whether a reader is guaranteed to see the latest write?
Nodes crash, disks fill up, and networks partition temporarily. How do replicas catch up after brief blips versus long outages, and how are conflicting writes reconciled?
expectations: Clarifies value size limits, point lookups versus range scans, single-region versus multi-region deployment, and tunable consistency needs.
Sizes cluster node count from 200 TB logical data multiplied by replication factor, compaction headroom, and per-node IOPS/throughput.
Partitions keys with consistent hashing and virtual nodes, replicating each key to `N` distinct failure domains via coordinator nodes.
Explains quorum reads and writes (`W + R > N` for overlap, smaller `W` or `R` for lower latency) and tracks membership via gossip or a consensus metadata service.
Designs the per-node storage engine around an append-only write-ahead log, an in-memory memtable, immutable sorted SSTables, background compaction, Bloom filters, and tombstones for deletes.
Resolves concurrent versions using vector clocks or last-write-wins timestamps (noting clock-skew risks) along with read repair.
Maintains availability and replica convergence through sloppy quorums with hinted handoff for transient failures and Merkle-tree anti-entropy sync for longer outages.
